- **(a) Sulfur dioxide, 24-hour mean:** **40 µg/m³** — this is the 2021 AQG level, defined at the 99th percentile of 24-hour means (i.e. 3–4 exceedance days per year).
- **(b) Nitrogen dioxide, annual mean:** **10 µg/m³** — this is the 2021 AQG level.

These are the final **AQG levels**, not the interim targets.

| Pollutant | Averaging time | IT1 | IT2 | IT3 | IT4 | AQG level |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| NO2 | 24-hour | 120 | 50 | – | – | 25 |

Footnote for 24-hour values: 99th percentile (3–4 exceedance days per year).

- NO2, 1-hour: **200 µg/m³** (from Global update 2005; not re-evaluated in 2021).

World Health Organization (2021). *WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide.* Geneva: World Health Organization. question: X19
answer:
ANSWER

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) requires no specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, no specific time period for counting them, and no specific lockout duration. All three are unfilled Assignment parameters — '[Assignment: organization-defined number]', '[Assignment: organization-defined time period]', and (inside part b) '[Assignment: organization-defined time period]' — and the lockout duration is not even mandatory, because locking is only one of five responses an organization may select. What the control requires is that the organization assign and enforce values; the values themselves come from the organization's risk decision, not from the publication.

Because the standard states no figure for any of the three asks, asks 1, 2 and 3 are reported in not_stated above, with the pages and search strings that establish the absence, and no figure is given for them.

1. AUTHORITATIVE CONTROL TEXT (verbatim)

Source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf, Chapter Three, page 99 (sha256 fc63bcd61715). Identical wording, apart from typographic ligature loss, in the SP 800-53 v5.1 derived-OSCAL PDF (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9) and the bsafes mirror (sha256 f9630cd5ebc4).

  AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS
  Control:
  a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon
     attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
  b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment:
     organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an
     administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay
     algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined
     action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.
  Discussion: The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the
  maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a
  local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts
  initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined,
  organization-defined time period. If a delay algorithm is selected, organizations may employ
  different algorithms for different components of the system based on the capabilities of those
  components. Responses to unsuccessful logon attempts may be implemented at both the operating
  system and the application levels.
  References: None.

(Note on the second quoted copy of this passage: the draft PDF, sha256 bdca6784056e, is a pre-final draft and uses 'account/node' and 'time-period' and omits the 'notify system administrator' selection. Do not quote the draft as the final requirement.)

2. WHY THERE IS NO NUMBER — PARAMETER MECHANICS

SP 800-53 control text is a template, not a fixed specification. Two parameter forms appear in AC-7:

  - Assignment: '[Assignment: organization-defined X]' marks a slot the organization must fill with its own value. The publication deliberately supplies no value. The draft's own explanation of the mechanism (sha256 bdca6784056e) states: 'While the parameter statements provide flexibility, organizations are responsible for choosing and assigning the parameters for each selected control. Once specified, the values for the assignment and selection statements become a permanent part of the control. The implementation of the control is assessed against the completed control statement.'
  - Selection: '[Selection (one or more): ...]' is a closed list the organization must choose from. Part b is a selection of five options: (i) lock the account or node for an organization-defined time period; (ii) lock until released by an administrator; (iii) delay the next logon prompt per an organization-defined delay algorithm; (iv) notify the system administrator; (v) take other organization-defined action.

Mapping to the three asks:

  Ask 1 (number of consecutive invalid logon attempts) -> AC-7(a), Assignment: organization-defined number. No value in the publication.
  Ask 2 (time period within which attempts are counted) -> AC-7(a), Assignment: organization-defined time period. No value in the publication.
  Ask 3 (lockout duration) -> AC-7(b) option (i), Assignment: organization-defined time period nested inside a Selection. No value in the publication, and the option itself is optional: an organization that selects option (ii), (iii), (iv) or (v) has no lockout duration at all.

Corollary: any specific figure presented as 'the AC-7 requirement' — including the attempt/window pairs sometimes attributed to AC-7 in secondary material — is not in the Rev. 5 control text. It is either an organizational assignment, a vendor default, or comes from a different document. I am not restating any such figure here, because the standard states none.

3. BASELINES DO NOT SUPPLY THE VALUES EITHER

Source: NIST SP 800-53B derived-OSCAL PDF (sha256 e5e3b616367e).

  - Table 3-1 (Access Control family) lists 'AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts  x x x' — the control is in the low-, moderate- and high-impact baselines (privacy baseline: not marked).
  - 'AC-7(1) AUTOMATIC ACCOUNT LOCK  W: Incorporated into AC-7.' The automatic-lock enhancement was withdrawn as a separate item and folded into base AC-7 part b.
  - SP 800-53B is a selection document: it says which controls apply at which impact level. It carries no parameter values, and the harness confirmed the strings 'invalid logon attempts', 'unsuccessful logon attempts' and 'failed logon attempts' do not appear anywhere in its 83,154 characters.
  - The Rev. 5 Update 1 landing page (sha256 e42d7c693146) records the 27 Aug 2025 Release 5.2.0 change list: new controls SA-15(13), SA-24, SI-02(07); revision to SI-07(12); discussion updates to SA-04, SA-05, SA-08, SA-08(14), SI-02, SI-02(05); related-control updates to all -01 controls and a named list. AC-7 is not in that list, so AC-7's text as quoted above stands for Rev. 5 / 5.1 / 5.2.0. (This is an inference from the published change list, not a re-read of the 5.2.0 body.)

4. WHAT AC-7 ACTUALLY OBLIGES — THE ENFORCEABLE REQUIREMENTS

Stripped of placeholders, an implementation is conformant only if all of the following hold:

  R1. A limit on consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user exists and is enforced — not merely documented (AC-7(a)).
  R2. The attempts are counted within a defined window (AC-7(a)).
  R3. On exceeding the limit, the system automatically takes at least one action from the part-b list — the action must be automatic, not manual (AC-7(b)).
  R4. Every bracket in the implemented statement is filled with a documented organizational value; an unfilled or 'TBD' parameter is a finding, because per the parameter mechanics the completed statement is what gets assessed.
  R5. The limit and the response apply regardless of whether the logon is local or network (Discussion).
  R6. Where a lockout is used, it is time-bounded by default or administratively released, because the Discussion warns of denial of service and states that automatic lockouts 'are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.'
  R7. Responses may be implemented at both the operating-system and application layers (Discussion); if both layers authenticate, both must be covered or the weaker layer becomes the bypass.

5. ENHANCEMENTS THAT ALSO CARRY PARAMETERS (all organization-defined)

  AC-7(2) PURGE OR WIPE MOBILE DEVICE — wipe after [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts; successful logons reset the count to zero; may be unnecessary where device data is strongly encrypted.
  AC-7(3) BIOMETRIC ATTEMPT LIMITING — limit unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [Assignment: organization-defined number].
  AC-7(4) USE OF ALTERNATE AUTHENTICATION FACTOR — allow [Assignment: organization-defined authentication factors] after the organization-defined consecutive invalid logon attempts are exceeded, and cap alternative-factor attempts at [Assignment: organization-defined number] within a [Assignment: organization-defined time period].
  AC-7(1) — withdrawn, incorporated into AC-7.

Related controls worth citing in the same SSP narrative: AC-2(3) (disable accounts after an organization-defined inactivity period), IA-5 (authenticator management), AU-6/AU-2 (auditing and review of the failure events the lockout generates), SC-5 (denial-of-service protection, the reason the Discussion favours temporary lockouts).

6. PROCEDURE — HOW THE THREE VALUES GET ANSWERED FOR A REAL SYSTEM

Since NIST does not supply the numbers, the deliverable for any actual system is a documented parameter assignment. Execute this and the three asks become answerable with system-specific figures:

  Step 1 — Confirm applicability. Check the system's impact level and confirm AC-7 is in the applicable baseline (it is in low, moderate and high per SP 800-53B Table 3-1).
  Step 2 — Choose the part-b response(s). Record the selection, e.g. 'lock the account or node for an organization-defined time period' or 'lock until released by an administrator'. At least one must be selected; more than one is permitted.
  Step 3 — Assign the parameters. Fill every bracket: attempt limit, counting window, lockout duration (or the administrator-release/delay-algorithm alternative), and, if AC-7(2)/(3)/(4) are selected, their numbers.
  Step 4 — Record the rationale. Tie each value to a risk decision (threat of online guessing versus the denial-of-service risk the Discussion names) and to any compensating control (MFA, rate limiting, anomaly alerting) that justifies the chosen threshold.
  Step 5 — Document in the SSP/control overlay. One row per parameter, with the fields below.
  Step 6 — Assess per SP 800-53A Rev. 5 against the completed statement, not the template: test that the configured value matches the documented value at every authentication layer.
  Step 7 — Review on a stated cadence and after any authentication-architecture change; a value assigned for a password-only system is not automatically valid after MFA is added.

Documentation record (use one row per parameter; this is the artefact that turns a placeholder into a requirement):

  Field                 | Content
  ----------------------+--------------------------------------------------------
  Control / parameter   | AC-7(a) attempt limit / AC-7(a) counting window / AC-7(b) response and its parameter
  OSCAL param reference | The OSCAL rendering of AC-7 exposes one parameter per bracket (conventionally ac-7_prm_1 ... ac-7_prm_n); confirm the exact IDs against the OSCAL catalog revision in use rather than assuming.
  Assigned value        | The organization's chosen value (number, duration, algorithm name, or 'administrator release')
  Unit                  | attempts / minutes or hours / n-a for a non-numeric selection
  Selection chosen      | Which part-b option(s) apply
  Rationale             | Risk basis, compensating controls, threat model reference
  Authority             | Who approved the assignment (system owner / authorizing official) and date
  Implementation locus  | OS, application, identity provider, or all — one row per layer
  Verification method   | Config check, log evidence, or test procedure used to prove enforcement
  Review cadence        | Date or trigger for reassignment

7. HOW TO REPRODUCE THIS ANSWER

  1. Open https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf and go to Chapter Three, page 99, 'AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS'. Confirm the three brackets and the five-option Selection in part b.
  2. Search the same PDF for 'lockout duration', 'account lockout duration', 'lockout period', 'time period that the account is locked', 'duration of the lockout' — none occurs (confirmed by the harness across all 492 pages).
  3. Open the SP 800-53B derived-OSCAL PDF, Table 3-1, and confirm 'AC-7 ... x x x' with no parameter column and 'AC-7(1) ... W: Incorporated into AC-7.'
  4. Optionally cross-check the v5.1 derived-OSCAL PDF (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9) — same wording, same absence of figures.

8. CAVEATS

  - SP 800-53 is a catalogue of controls; it is not a configuration benchmark. A system that must meet a fixed numeric lockout threshold is being driven by something else — an organizational policy, a regulator, a binding operational directive, a vendor hardening guide, or an overlay — and that source, not AC-7, is where the figure should be cited from.
  - The Rev. 5 draft PDF should not be quoted as authoritative: it differs from the final in part b (no 'notify system administrator' option; 'account/node' and 'time-period' wording).
  - If the requester's real need is a defensible starting value for a system, that is an organizational risk decision plus possibly other NIST publications outside the grounding used here; I have deliberately not substituted a number for the three asks, because the standard states none.

answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — Australian LIPD class licence, 2400–2483.5 MHz, 'digital modulation' transmitters, as at 17 November 2026

1. IDENTIFYING THE INSTRUMENT IN FORCE (Ask 1 constraint; Ask 4)

Instrument: Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025.
Federal Register of Legislation ID: F2025L01047. Authorised version registered 05/09/2025.

Basis for 'in force on 17 November 2026':
- The Federal Register of Legislation page https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text carries the header 'Authorised Version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025' and the body heading 'Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025'.
- The ACMA's LIPD class licence page (https://www.acma.gov.au/licences/low-interference-potential-devices-lipd-class-licence, 'Last updated: 02 October 2025') states that users 'must follow all the rules in the: Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025' and names that instrument again in its body.
- The predecessor, the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015 (F2005B00339), is superseded; the 2025 licence replaces it. (Note: one secondary commercial page still cites 'Class Licence 2015 … last updated in May 2023' and Section 55/56/59 numbering; that page is out of date on the instrument's identity and its section numbering must not be relied on. Its limit values nevertheless match the 2025 licence.)

Year of making carried in the name: 2025.

Residual verification step for the responsible engineer (record it in the compliance file): confirm on the Federal Register of Legislation that no amending instrument was registered between 05/09/2025 and 17/11/2026 and that F2025L01047 is the compilation in force on that date. The grounding (fetched 25/11/2026, i.e. after the target date) shows no such amendment and shows the 2025 licence as the operative one.

2. MAXIMUM EIRP FOR 'DIGITAL MODULATION' IN 2400–2483.5 MHz (Ask 2)

Source: Schedule 1, Part 8 (Frequency hopping, WiFi and RLAN transmitters), clause 38, Table 8, item 7.

Verbatim table row (columns: Class of transmitter | Permitted operating frequency band | Maximum EIRP | Additional limitations):
  7 | Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43

Clause 38 states: 'No additional requirements apply to Table 8' beyond the clause-referenced additional limitations in column 4.

ANSWER: Maximum EIRP = 4 W (i.e. 4 watts EIRP; equivalently 36.0 dBm EIRP).

3. ADDITIONAL LIMIT ON RADIATED PEAK POWER SPECTRAL DENSITY (Ask 3)

Source: clause 43 (additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9 — the digital modulation items at 915–928 MHz, 2400–2483.5 MHz and the third digital-modulation band).

Verbatim: 'A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz.'

ANSWER: Radiated peak power spectral density must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz (equivalently 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz; 8.33 W/MHz or 39.21 dBm/MHz if a per-MHz presentation is needed for comparison with other regimes — the instrument's own unit is mW per 3 kHz and that is the unit of record).

This clause is the only additional limitation attached to Table 8 item 7; there is no indoor-only restriction, no DFS requirement and no elevation-dependent restriction for that item (those attach to other items, e.g. clauses 44–46).

4. HOW TO APPLY THE TWO LIMITS TOGETHER (verification that the stated figures are mutually consistent)

A digital modulation transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz must satisfy BOTH:
  (a) total EIRP ≤ 4 W (36.0 dBm); and
  (b) radiated peak PSD ≤ 25 mW per 3 kHz (13.98 dBm/3 kHz).

Consistency check: 25 mW per 3 kHz expressed per MHz is 25 mW × (1000/3) = 8.33 W/MHz = 39.21 dBm/MHz, which is above the 36.0 dBm total EIRP cap. Therefore for any emission wider than about 1.15 MHz the total-EIRP cap binds first and the PSD limit is automatically met; for narrowband emissions (below ~1.15 MHz) the PSD limit binds first. Worked examples:
  - 20 MHz wide signal at the 4 W EIRP cap → 36.0 dBm − 10·log10(20 MHz / 1 MHz) = 36.0 − 13.01 = 22.99 dBm/MHz, i.e. ~200 mW/MHz, far below the 8.33 W/MHz PSD ceiling. Compliant on both counts.
  - 1 MHz wide signal at 4 W EIRP → 36.0 dBm/MHz vs PSD ceiling 39.21 dBm/MHz. Compliant on both counts.
  - 1 kHz wide signal at 4 W EIRP → 36.0 dBm in 1 kHz, versus a PSD ceiling of 13.98 dBm/3 kHz (≈ 9.2 dBm/kHz). Non-compliant on PSD; the PSD limit governs and the permitted power is roughly 9 dBm in 1 kHz.

5. ITEMS IN THE SAME BAND THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH THIS ONE

  - Table 8 item 2: frequency hopping, 2400–2483.5 MHz, 500 mW, see clause 40.
  - Table 8 item 3: frequency hopping, 2400–2483.5 MHz, 4 W, see clause 41.
  - A separate generic table row reading 'Any | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 10 mW | None' — this is a different (low-power, any-device) item, not the digital modulation class. Equipment assessed against 10 mW when it in fact falls in the digital modulation class would be under-stated by 26 dB.
  - Table 8 items 8, 10 and 11 (5150–5250 MHz etc.) carry their own additional limitations (clauses 44, 45, 46) including indoor-only and DFS; none of those apply to the 2.4 GHz digital modulation item.

6. SECONDARY CORROBORATION

An independent commercial compilation (Powertec, 'AU 2400-2483.5 MHz') states for Australia: Max EIRP 4 W, and for 'Digital modulation transmitters, 4 Watts' the condition 'The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz.' This agrees with the licence text on both figures.

7. COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (apply directly to a product assessment)

Step 1 — Classify: confirm the transmitter is a 'digital modulation' radiocommunications transmitter (i.e. it uses digital modulation rather than frequency hopping) operating wholly within 2400–2483.5 MHz. If it is a frequency hopping transmitter, use Table 8 items 2/3 instead.
Step 2 — EIRP test: compute maximum EIRP = conducted output power (dBm) + antenna gain (dBi) − cable/feeder loss (dB). Pass if ≤ 36.0 dBm (4 W). Record the antenna(s) assessed, since EIRP depends on the antenna fitted.
Step 3 — PSD test: measure or compute radiated peak PSD in any 3 kHz. Pass if ≤ 25 mW per 3 kHz (13.98 dBm per 3 kHz). Use the 3 kHz reference bandwidth stated in the instrument, not 1 MHz, when testing against this limit.
Step 4 — Other obligations outside this licence item still apply and are not covered by this determination: the ACMA General Equipment Rules (including Schedule 5 general standards and Schedule 4 EME standard), the Radiocommunications (Electromagnetic Compatibility) Standard 2017, and the Murchison Radioastronomy Observatory exclusion zone (70 km radius, central Western Australia) restrictions on LIPD operation.
Step 5 — File the determination with: instrument name and FRL ID (F2025L01047), registration date 05/09/2025, table/clause references (Table 8 item 7; clause 43), the two limit values, the antenna configuration, and the date-of-assessment check that this is the compilation in force.

8. ANSWERS

Ask 2 — Maximum EIRP for a digital modulation transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz: 4 W (36.0 dBm).
Ask 3 — Additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density: 25 mW per 3 kHz (13.98 dBm per 3 kHz).
Ask 4 — Year of making of the instrument in force, carried in its name: 2025 (Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025, F2025L01047, registered 05/09/2025).

question: X35
answer:
RYDBERG CONSTANT R∞ — CODATA 2022 RECOMMENDED VALUE, ITS STANDARD UNCERTAINTY, AND THE CODATA 2018 VALUE IT REPLACED

1. ANSWERS (quoted verbatim from NIST, not recalculated)

  Ask 1 — CODATA 2022 recommended value of R∞:
      R∞ = 10 973 731.568 157 m^-1
      Concise form as published: 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1

  Ask 2 — its standard uncertainty (absolute, one standard deviation, in m^-1):
      u(R∞) = 0.000 012 m^-1
      (the "(12)" in the concise form is the one-sigma uncertainty in the last two digits, per the NIST SP 961 note: "a number in parentheses, if present, is the one-standard-deviation uncertainty in the last two digits")
      Published relative standard uncertainty, given for completeness: 1.1 x 10^-12 (dimensionless)

  Ask 3 — the CODATA 2018 value that the 2022 value replaced:
      R∞ (2018) = 10 973 731.568 160 m^-1
      Concise form as published: 10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1
      (2018 standard uncertainty, read from the same published notation: 0.000 021 m^-1; this was not requested and is supplied only as the paired figure from the same line)

2. SOURCES OF RECORD (with what each actually prints)

  a) NIST CODATA database, value page for the Rydberg constant,
     https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?ryd  (accessed 2026-11-25):
        Numerical value                10 973 731.568 157   m-1
        Standard uncertainty                     0.000 012   m-1
        Relative standard uncertainty            1.1 x 10-12
        Concise form                   10 973 731.568 157(12)   m-1
        "Source: 2022 CODATA recommended values"
     This page is the primary source for asks 1 and 2.

  b) NIST SP 961 (May 2024), CODATA RECOMMENDED VALUES OF THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL CONSTANTS: 2022,
     https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2022.pdf:
        "Rydberg constant  R∞  10 973 731.568 157(12) [m−1]"
     Cross-check for ask 1 (agrees digit for digit with (a)).

  c) NIST, Fundamental Physical Constants — Extensive Listing, 2022 CODATA adjustment,
     https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/all.pdf, and the Atomic and nuclear constants category PDF,
     https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Category?view=pdf&Atomic+and+nuclear.x=116&Atomic+and+nuclear.y=15:
        "Rydberg constant  R∞  10 973 731.568 157(12) [m−1]  1.1 × 10−12"
     Cross-check for ask 1 and for the relative uncertainty.

  d) NIST SP 961 (May 2019), CODATA RECOMMENDED VALUES OF THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL CONSTANTS: 2018,
     https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2018.pdf:
        "Rydberg constant  R∞  10 973 731.568 160(21) [m−1]"
     This is the source for ask 3. It is the 2018 wall chart, not the current 2022 pages.

  e) NIST, Version history of the fundamental constants database,
     https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Reference/versioncon.shtml (accessed 2026-11-25):
        "Version 9.0  9 May 2024  Values updated to the 2022 CODATA recommended values. The 2022 values replace the previously recommended 2018 CODATA values, which are available in archived tables."
        "Version 8.0  20 May 2019  Values updated to the 2018 CODATA recommended values."
     This establishes the replacement relation asserted in ask 3.

  Suggested citation string for a report:
     E. Tiesinga, P. J. Mohr, D. B. Newell, and B. N. Taylor (2024), "The 2022 CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants" (Web Version 9.0), NIST, Gaithersburg, MD 20899; database at https://physics.nist.gov/constants; R∞ page https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?ryd, accessed 2026-11-25. 2018 value from NIST SP 961 (May 2019) CODATA 2018 wall chart, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2018.pdf.

3. UNIT AND NOTATION NOTES (metrological caveats that must travel with these numbers)

  - Unit. The published unit is written [m−1] with square brackets, and NIST's footnote on the wall charts and listings defines it: "For units with square brackets the full descriptions of [m]−1 and [m] are cycles per meter and meter per cycle, respectively." The value page adds: "The full description of unit m-1 is cycles or periods per meter." So R∞ = 10 973 731.568 157 cycles per metre; in the current SI, where angles are dimensionless, this is numerically the same as 10 973 731.568 157 m^-1 and no conversion factor is applied. Report it as m^-1 (cycles per metre) and do not silently re-express it as a radian-based wavenumber.

  - Which uncertainty. 'Standard uncertainty' in the NIST tables is the absolute one-standard-deviation uncertainty in the unit of the value: 0.000 012 m^-1. The separate published quantity 'relative standard uncertainty' is 1.1 x 10^-12 (dimensionless). Both are quoted above so that neither can be mistaken for the other. Internal check: 0.000 012 / 10 973 731.568 157 = 1.09 x 10^-12, which rounds to the published 1.1 x 10^-12 — the two published figures are mutually consistent.

  - Precision. Values are quoted at full published precision, exactly as digit-printed, with NIST's digit grouping (spaces as thousands separators; the SI/ISO style of grouping in threes). Do not round to fewer digits when transcribing; the last two digits are the uncertainty-bearing digits.

  - Do not recalculate. R∞ can be derived from α, m_e, h, c, but the recommended value is the output of the CODATA least-squares adjustment; a recomputation from rounded constants will not reproduce the published digits. Quote, do not derive.

4. 2018 -> 2022 COMPARISON (optional note; the request asked only for the 2018 value)

  Value:        2018  10 973 731.568 160 m^-1
                2022  10 973 731.568 157 m^-1
  Difference:   2022 - 2018 = -0.000 003 m^-1 = -3 x 10^-6 m^-1
  Relative:     -3 x 10^-6 / 10 973 731.568 160 = -2.7 x 10^-13
  In sigma:     |difference| = 0.25 x u(2022)  [0.000 003 / 0.000 012 = 0.25]
                |difference| is about 0.14 x u(2018)  [0.000 003 / 0.000 021 = 0.14]
  Interpretation: the shift is smaller than either standard uncertainty, so the 2022 and 2018 recommended values are consistent within their stated uncertainties; the move is a refinement of precision (u: 0.000 021 -> 0.000 012 m^-1, a factor 1.75 improvement) rather than a correction of the central value.

5. HOW TO STATE IT IN ONE SENTENCE

question: X36
answer:
BOTTOM LINE

NASA-STD-4003A (w/CHANGE 1) does not state a maximum RF impedance in ohms at any frequency for a Class R bond joint. There is no number to quote. The Class R requirement is a performance/design requirement — the bond path and each joint in it must have inductance and overall impedance (including resonances) low enough to prevent interference at the program's frequencies of interest — plus one numeric limit, which is a dc resistance: 2.5 milliohms (0.0025 Ω) maximum across each joint in the path.

Answering the designer's question with '2.5 mΩ at <frequency>' would be wrong twice over: wrong quantity (dc resistance, not RF impedance) and wrong inference (the standard's own Appendix says a joint under 2.5 mΩ dc is not thereby a good RF bond).


1. WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY SAYS (verbatim, NASA-STD-4003A w/CHANGE 1, §4.1.4)

'4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)
The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.

a. [EBR 20] All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.

b. [EBR 21] All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.

(1) [EBR 22] The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.

c. [EBR 23] The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.'

The requirement table in the same document restates these as 4.1.4a/EBR 20, 4.1.4b/EBR 21, 4.1.4b(1)/EBR 22, 4.1.4c/EBR 23 — so EBR 21 and EBR 22 are the citable paragraph identifiers for a compliance document.

Governing numeric value, Class R:

    R_dc ≤ 2.5 mΩ = 0.0025 Ω  across EACH JOINT in the path  (EBR 22)

Nothing else in Class R is numeric. There is no ohms-per-frequency figure, no transfer-impedance figure, no reactance limit, and no measurement frequency.

Supporting design constraints that do bound RF behaviour (all Class R, all citable):
- 5.1.2b [EBR 66]: 'For Class R bonds, the bonding straps shall be as short as possible.'
- 5.1.2b(2) [EBR 68]: 'The bond straps shall have a length-to-width ratio of less than 5 to 1 to minimize the inductance of the strap.'
- Table 1 (Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes), Class R row (also present in the historical baseline): 'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.'


2. WHY THERE IS NO RF IMPEDANCE NUMBER — THE STANDARD'S OWN RATIONALE (Appendix B.3.4)

The Appendix is explicit that the dc number is not an RF criterion:

'The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond.'

And it describes the impedance-vs-frequency behaviour that the designer must actually control:

'The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance. The impedance due to inductance then increases at 20 dB per decade of frequency to a frequency where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal. At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit. The Q is high when the resistance is low, which is usually the case for a bonding joint. At frequencies above this point, the capacitive reactance is less than the inductive reactance; and the total impedance begins to come back down.'

'The equivalent resistance includes the resistance of any bond strap present plus the resistance of the joints in the path. At higher frequencies, where the diameter or thickness of the strap significantly exceeds the skin depth, the ac resistance becomes larger than the dc resistance. The ac resistance increases with the square root of frequency.'

This is exactly why a single RF impedance limit at a single frequency cannot be written into a general bonding standard: the impedance is geometry- and frequency-dependent, is dominated by inductance above a few kHz, and is dominated by a parallel resonance of unpredictable Q at higher frequency. The standard therefore sets a measurable dc screen (2.5 mΩ/joint) and pushes the RF impedance target to the program ('frequencies of interest').


3. HISTORICAL CONSISTENCY (so the designer can cite either revision)

NASA-STD-4003 (Sept 2003), §4.3: 'Basic structure and vehicle skin shall be designed and constructed to provide a uniform low-impedance path at radio frequencies so that system operational requirements are met. RF bonding is required between all conductive basic structural components of the vehicle. The dc resistance across each joint shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms... The dc resistance from equipment case to structure shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms. The bond from the equipment enclosure to any mounting plate furnished with the equipment shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms. The path to structure and the joints in that path shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance including resonances are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.'

NASA-STD-4003A (un-changed baseline), §4.1.4b(1): 'The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.'

The 2.5 mΩ figure has been stable across 4003, 4003A, and 4003A w/CHANGE 1, and matches the companion guidance (NTRS 19970005154, C.2.3.5.2): 'The actual requirement is a maximum resistance of the Class R bond of 2.5 milliohms.' No revision anywhere in the fetched text carries an RF impedance value.


4. THE CONSTRAINT ON THE JOINT (ask 3) — READ THE SCOPE WORD 'EACH'

EBR 22 is a per-joint limit, not a per-path limit: 'across each joint in the path.' Implications for a designer:
- A path of equipment case → mounting plate → bracket → structure has three joints and therefore three independent 2.5 mΩ allowances. The path total is not required to be ≤ 2.5 mΩ; the standard bounds it only by EBR 21 (low enough impedance at the frequencies of interest).
- The historical text additionally fixes the equipment case-to-structure bond and the equipment-to-mounting-plate bond at 2.5 mΩ each.
- If the joint serves more than one class (e.g., Class R for RF and Class H for fault current), the standard requires meeting the strictest applicable class or the strictest requirements of each — a Class R/H joint must be low-inductance with ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc AND have adequate contact area for the maximum fault current.
- Class R also applies to the outer mold line (EBR 23): OML component-to-component bonds must present a uniform low-impedance enclosure.


5. HOW THE REQUIREMENT IS VERIFIED (relevant because the designer will have to close it)

From the verification section of 4003A w/CHANGE 1:
- 'The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds.' (Other bonds of the same type, same process, may be verified by similarity; spot checks confirm the process is still good.)
- 'Low inductance paths of Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection.'

So the closure package for a Class R joint is:
(a) dc resistance evidence — four-wire (Kelvin) milliohm measurement on a sample joint built with the flight process, showing ≤ 2.5 mΩ, plus similarity/spot-check records;
(b) low-inductance evidence — a written analysis of the geometry (strap length, width, thickness, joint overlap area, number of parallel paths, presence of any jumper or pigtail) plus a drawing inspection confirming the 5:1 length-to-width rule (EBR 68) and shortest-possible strap (EBR 66), and confirming direct metal-to-metal contact where used.
There is no RF impedance measurement to pass, because there is no RF impedance limit to pass.


6. IF THE PROGRAM NEEDS A NUMBER: DERIVING AN RF IMPEDANCE TARGET (do not attribute it to 4003A)

EBR 21 is a requirement to derive and meet a number, not a number. The number comes from the program's EMI/EMC control plan or a subsystem allocation, and must be flowed down and cited as a program-derived requirement, with EBR 21 as the parent. Procedure:

Step 1 — Fix the frequencies of interest. Take f_min..f_max from the emitter/victim set (transmitter bands, receiver bands, digital clock harmonics, transient spectra). This is the 'stated frequency' the standard deliberately leaves open.

Step 2 — Allocate Z_allow(f). Typical allocations: a small fraction of the shield-termination impedance, or a fraction of the enclosure transfer impedance target, or a value that keeps the common-mode voltage developed across the bond below the victim's susceptibility threshold. Record the allocation and its source.

Step 3 — Compute the bond inductance from geometry. For a straight flat strap of length l, width w, thickness t (all in cm), inductance in µH:

    L(µH) = 0.002 · l · [ ln( 2l / (w + t) ) + 0.5 + 0.2235 · (w + t) / l ]

Add the joint spreading inductance and any pigtail/jumper inductance separately (a round pigtail of length l and diameter d: L ≈ 0.2·l·[ln(4l/d) − 1] nH with l, d in mm).

Step 4 — Check |Z(f)| = sqrt(R_dc² + (2πfL)²) against Z_allow at f_max, and check for a parallel resonance between the bond inductance and the local stray capacitance; at high Q the impedance can rise to 'thousands of ohms' (Appendix B.3.4). Damping (lossy joint, resistive contact, added loss) may be needed.

Step 5 — If the check fails: shorten and widen the strap, go to direct metal-to-metal contact over a large area, or parallel multiple straps. Do not attempt to fix an RF problem by polishing the dc resistance.

Worked illustration (shows why 2.5 mΩ cannot be read as an RF limit):
Strap 50 mm long × 10 mm wide × 0.5 mm thick, i.e. exactly at the 5:1 limit (EBR 68):
  l = 5 cm, w = 1 cm, t = 0.05 cm
  2l/(w+t) = 10/1.05 = 9.524 → ln = 2.254
  0.2235·(w+t)/l = 0.2235·1.05/5 = 0.0469
  L = 0.002 · 5 · (2.254 + 0.5 + 0.0469) = 0.0280 µH = 28.0 nH

  Breakpoint where ωL = R_dc = 2.5 mΩ:  f = R/(2πL) = 0.0025/(2π·28.0e-9) = 14.2 kHz

  |Z| vs frequency for this compliant joint (R = 2.5 mΩ, L = 28.0 nH):
    1 kHz      ωL = 0.176 mΩ   |Z| ≈ 2.51 mΩ
    14.2 kHz   ωL = 2.5 mΩ     |Z| ≈ 3.54 mΩ
    100 kHz    ωL = 17.6 mΩ    |Z| ≈ 17.8 mΩ
    1 MHz      ωL = 176 mΩ     |Z| ≈ 176 mΩ
    10 MHz     ωL = 1.76 Ω      |Z| ≈ 1.76 Ω
    100 MHz    ωL = 17.6 Ω      |Z| ≈ 17.6 Ω

The joint passes EBR 22 by construction and is still ~17.6 Ω at 100 MHz — seven thousand times the dc limit. This is precisely the failure mode the Appendix warns about.

Corollary worth showing the designer: to hold |Z| ≤ 2.5 mΩ all the way to 100 MHz you would need L ≤ R/(2πf) = 0.0025/(2π·1e8) = 3.98 pH, which is not physically achievable in a bolted or strapped joint. That is the reason the standard does not, and cannot, state a single RF impedance limit.


7. WHAT TO PUT IN THE COMPLIANCE DOCUMENT

Correct citation form for a Class R bond joint:

  'Class R electrical bond, NASA-STD-4003A w/CHANGE 1, §4.1.4b [EBR 21]: bond path and joints designed for low inductance and low overall impedance, including resonances, at the frequencies of interest. §4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22]: dc resistance across each joint ≤ 2.5 mΩ. Compliance: dc resistance verified by sample-bond test (≤ 2.5 mΩ, four-wire); low-inductance path verified by analysis and inspection per §6, including §5.1.2b [EBR 66] (straps as short as possible) and §5.1.2b(2) [EBR 68] (length-to-width < 5:1).'

Do NOT write 'Class R RF impedance ≤ ___ Ω at ___ MHz per NASA-STD-4003A.' That sentence has no basis in the standard. If a program-specific RF impedance number exists, cite it as a program-derived allocation from EBR 21, with the deriving document and the allocation calculation attached.


8. CAVEATS AND TAILORING

- 4003A is tailorable: 'Individual provisions of this standard may be tailored (i.e. modified or deleted) by contract or program specifications.' A program may impose a numeric RF impedance limit; that limit would be a program requirement, not a 4003A requirement, and should be cited as such.
- The standard does not supersede other Agency requirements; conflicts are resolved by the responsible Technical Authority (§2.4).
- Nothing in the fetched text of 4003, 4003A, or 4003A w/CHANGE 1 specifies an RF impedance measurement instrument, a test frequency, or an RF acceptance criterion for Class R joints. If a reviewer asks for one, the answer is that it is a derived requirement, not a standard requirement.
- Revision to cite: NASA-STD-4003A w/CHANGE 1 (current revalidated controlled copy). Confirm the program's contractual revision before quoting paragraph numbers, since numbering shifted between 4003 (§4.3) and 4003A (§4.1.4).

The first reads: "47 TABLE LIST OF TABLES PAGE 1 Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes .............................................................."

# AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) — parameter determination, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5

## Bottom line

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, control AC-7 **does not require any specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, any specific time period, or any specific lockout duration.** All three are *assignment parameters* — blanks the control deliberately leaves for the organization to fill in its security plan. There is no figure in AC-7, in any AC-7 enhancement, or anywhere else in the publication for these three quantities. Anyone quoting "N attempts / M minutes / K-minute lockout" as a requirement of 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-7 is quoting an overlay (agency policy, a FedRAMP-style parameter set, or a vendor baseline), not the NIST control.

## The control text, verbatim (Rev. 5 / 5.1, AC-7)

> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

Discussion (same control): "Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period." That is the only time-related statement, and it too is a placeholder.

## Mapping of each ask to the control

| Ask | AC-7 element | Slot in the control | Value stated by NIST |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | AC-7a, first parameter | `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` | **None — organization-defined** |
| 2. Time period within which the attempts are counted | AC-7a, second parameter | `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` | **None — organization-defined** |
| 3. Lockout duration | AC-7b, first selection option, its parameter | `lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]` | **None — organization-defined**, and only applicable if account/node lockout is the option the organization selects |

Two structural points that matter for implementation and for assessment:

1. **The count window in ask 2 is not the same thing as the lockout period in ask 3.** AC-7a's time period bounds the counting of consecutive failures; AC-7b's time period bounds how long the lock lasts once the limit is exceeded. They are independent parameters and must be documented as two separate values.
2. **Lockout is not mandatory.** AC-7b is a *selection (one or more)*. An organization may satisfy it with an administrator-release lock, a delay algorithm on the next logon prompt, administrator notification, or another organization-defined action — with no timed lockout at all. Ask 3 therefore has no answer even in principle unless the organization has selected the timed-lockout option.

## Corroboration across the fetched copies

Three independent renderings of the control in the grounding all carry the identical placeholder wording and none carries a figure: the NIST publication PDF (nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-53r5.pdf, sha256 fc63bcd61715), the OSCAL-derived Rev. 5.1 PDF (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9), and the bsafes mirror of the AC-7 page (sha256 f9630cd5ebc4). The draft (sha256 d1fd2107db9d) is the same. The enhancements are equally placeholder-only: AC-7(2) purge/wipe after `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts; AC-7(3) biometric attempt limit `[Assignment: organization-defined number]`; AC-7(4)(b) `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` attempts over an `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` using alternate factors. AC-7(1) (automatic account lock) was withdrawn and incorporated into AC-7.

Searches confirming absence, as run by the harness over full page text: 'duration', 'lockout duration', 'lockout time period' and 'account lockout duration' appear in none of the OSCAL-derived 800-53r5 PDF (396 pages), the CSRC Rev. 5 landing page, the bsafes AC-7 page, or the draft baselines markup; 'time period'/'time' appear in none of the CSRC Rev. 5 landing page; 'invalid logon attempts'/'unsuccessful logon attempts' appear in none of the CSRC Rev. 5 landing page. The landing page is a publication index, which is why the phrase-level searches miss there — but the control-text copies, where the phrases do occur, contain them only inside assignment brackets.

## What an implementer must therefore produce (the actual engineering work)

Since NIST supplies no figures, AC-7 compliance is achieved by *deciding, documenting and enforcing* the three parameters. Minimum deliverable set for a system security plan or control implementation statement:

| Parameter to record | Source of the decision | Where it is recorded | Enforcement point |
|---|---|---|---|

# LIPD Class Licence — 'digital modulation' transmitters in 2400–2483.5 MHz
## Regulatory answer sheet, stated as at 17 November 2026

---

## 0. Bottom line

| Ask | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Maximum EIRP for a 'digital modulation' transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz | **4 W** (= 4000 mW = **36.0 dBm EIRP**) |
| 3 | Additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density for that class | **25 mW per 3 kHz** (= **13.98 dBm per 3 kHz**) |
| 4 | Year carried in the name of the instrument now in force | **2015** — *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015* |

The 4 W figure is the EIRP ceiling; the 25 mW/3 kHz figure is a **separate, cumulative** constraint. A transmitter must satisfy both. In practice the PSD limit, not the 4 W ceiling, is what binds any transmitter whose occupied bandwidth is under about 480 kHz (see §3.3).

---

## 1. Instrument identification (the ask-1 constraint)

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| Title | *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015* |
| FRLI identifier | F2015L01438 |
| Enabling provision | section 132, *Radiocommunications Act 1992* (Cth) |
| Registered | 15 September 2015 |
| Commenced | 16 September 2015 |
| Latest compilation in evidence | F2023C00524, registered 29 June 2023 |
| Amended by (in evidence) | Variations 2016 (No. 1) [F2016L00636], 2018 (No. 1), 2019 (No. 1), 2020 (No. 1), 2021 (No. 1) [F2021L00449] |

Operating rule that makes the Schedule 1 table binding — the licensee must ensure the transmitter is operated:

> "(i) on a frequency, or within a range of frequencies, mentioned in column 2 of the item; (ii) at a radiated power that does not exceed the maximum EIRP mentioned in column 3 of the item; and (iii) in accordance with the limitations (if any) mentioned in column 4 of the item;"

Definition of the ceiling (dictionary to the licence):

> "**maximum EIRP**, for a transmitter mentioned in column 1 of an item in Schedule 1, means the largest amount of EIRP, mentioned in column 3 of that item, that may be radiated by the transmitter in any direction."

Band convention (column 2 heading): "Permitted operating frequency band (MHz) (lower limit exclusive, upper limit inclusive)" — so the authorised range is the half-open interval **(2400, 2483.5] MHz**. Operation exactly at 2400.000 MHz is outside; operation exactly at 2483.5 MHz is inside.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — maximum EIRP

Schedule 1, **item 59**, reproduced verbatim from the in-force compilation:

| Column 1 — Class of transmitter | Column 2 — Permitted operating frequency band (MHz) | Column 3 — Maximum EIRP | Column 4 — Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Digital modulation transmitters | 2400–2483.5 | **4 W** | The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz. |

**Answer: 4 W EIRP.**

Conversions for the design file:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Maximum EIRP | 4 W |
| in milliwatts | 4 000 mW |
| in dBm | 10·log10(4000) = **36.02 dBm** (round to 36.0 dBm) |
| Applicable directions | any direction (definition of *maximum EIRP*, above) — the 4 W is not a per-sector or per-beam allowance |
| Basis | radiated (EIRP), not conducted transmitter power; antenna gain counts |

### 2.1 The 10 mW row is NOT the answer

Schedule 1 item 21 reads "All transmitters | 2400–2483.5 | 10 mW". That is the general fallback class for transmitters that do not fall within a more specific class. A device that is a *digital modulation transmitter* in this band is authorised by the specific item 59 at 4 W. Quoting 10 mW for such a device is the standard misread and would understate the permitted EIRP by a factor of 400 (26 dB).

---

## 3. Ask 3 — additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density

Column 4 of item 59, verbatim, in force:

> "The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz."

**Answer: 25 mW per 3 kHz.**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Limit | 25 mW per 3 kHz |
| in dBm per 3 kHz | 10·log10(25) = **13.98 dBm per 3 kHz** (≈ 14 dBm/3 kHz) |
| Detector / statistic | **peak** (not average, not mean) |
| Measurement bandwidth | **any 3 kHz** — worst-case 3 kHz segment anywhere within the emission |
| Reference plane | **radiated** (EIRP basis); a conducted PSD figure must have the antenna gain added before comparison |
| Averaging window | none specified — treat as peak envelope; do not average across a burst or across hopping channels |

### 3.1 This is the only column-4 limitation for item 59

The original 2015 text carried a second limitation, "(b) The minimum 6 dB bandwidth must be at least 500 kHz." The *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence Variation 2016 (No. 1)* removed it, and the explanatory statement to that variation says so expressly:

> "Item 5 – Schedule 1, item 59, column 4 … removes the existing limitation at paragraph (b). The only limitation retained is that the radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz."

So a 2015-era datasheet or an older copy of the licence that quotes a 500 kHz minimum bandwidth is out of date. There is no minimum-bandwidth condition today.

### 3.2 Limits that do NOT apply to item 59

For completeness, and to stop over-application of neighbouring rows:

- **No Transmit Power Control (TPC) requirement.** TPC appears only in the RLAN rows (items 61–63).
- **No Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) requirement.** Same — RLAN rows only.
- **No indoor-only restriction.** The indoor-only condition applies to items 61, 62 and 63AA, not to item 59.
- **No frequency-hopping minimum-channel-count condition.** That is item 57 (5725–5850 MHz, 4 W, ≥75 hopping frequencies).

### 3.3 Engineering consequence: which limit binds

Both limits apply simultaneously. For a flat-emission approximation, the highest EIRP that satisfies the PSD limit over an occupied bandwidth *B* is:

    EIRP_PSD(B) = 25 mW × (B / 3 kHz)

Setting that equal to 4 W gives the crossover bandwidth:

    B* = 3 kHz × (4000 mW / 25 mW) = 3 kHz × 160 = 480 kHz

In decibels: 36.02 − 13.98 = 22.04 dB, and 10^(22.04/10) = 160, so B* = 160 × 3 kHz = 480 kHz.

| Occupied bandwidth B | PSD-permitted EIRP, 25 mW × B/3 kHz | Governing limit | Permitted EIRP |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 kHz | 25 mW (14.0 dBm) | PSD | 25 mW |
| 10 kHz | 83.3 mW (19.2 dBm) | PSD | 83.3 mW |
| 100 kHz | 833 mW (29.2 dBm) | PSD | 833 mW |
| 480 kHz | 4.0 W (36.0 dBm) | both, coincident | 4.0 W |
| 1 MHz | 8.33 W (39.2 dBm) | EIRP ceiling | **4 W** |
| 20 MHz | 166.7 W (52.2 dBm) | EIRP ceiling | **4 W** |

Design rules that follow directly:

1. **Narrowband designs are PSD-limited, not EIRP-limited.** A 100 kHz-wide link tops out near 833 mW EIRP (29.2 dBm), not 4 W.
2. **Wideband designs are EIRP-limited.** Anything at or above roughly 480 kHz occupied bandwidth can use the full 4 W, provided the emission is flat enough that no 3 kHz slice exceeds 25 mW.
3. **Spectral flatness matters as much as total power.** A 4 W emission with a 10 dB peak-to-average spectral ripple will breach the 3 kHz limit even though total EIRP is compliant. Compliance testing must sweep a 3 kHz window across the emission and take the worst case.
4. **Illustrative only:** 25 mW/3 kHz normalises to 39.2 dBm/MHz (13.98 dBm + 10·log10(1000/3)). This is a convenience figure for comparing against per-MHz rules elsewhere; the enforceable limit remains expressed per 3 kHz.

---

## 4. Ask 4 — year of the instrument in force

**2015.** The instrument made, registered and in force on the evidence available is the *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence **2015*** (F2015L01438), which states of itself: "This Class Licence is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015." Registered 15 September 2015; commenced 16 September 2015; current compilation in evidence F2023C00524 (registered 29 June 2023).

### 4.1 The 2025 document in circulation is a consultation draft, not a made instrument

The ACMA has published a *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025* marked **"DRAFT FOR CONSULTATION"** on every page. A draft released for comment is not an instrument made under s 132 and is not in force. On the material available, the year carried by the name of the instrument in force is **2015**.

### 4.2 Verification note (does not change asks 2 or 3)

The 2015 instrument is subject to sunsetting under Part 4 of the *Legislation Act 2003* — ten years from registration (15 September 2015) falls in September 2025, and the applicable sunset day would be 1 October 2025 — so a remake could well be in force by 17 November 2026, in which case the title year would read **2025**. Two things follow:

- **Confirm the point-in-time position on the Federal Register of Legislation** (series F2015L01438 and any successor 2025 series) for the actual date of reliance, rather than relying on this sheet alone.
- **The confirmation cannot change asks 2 or 3.** The draft 2025 instrument reproduces identical figures: Schedule 1 item 7, "Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43", and clause 43 reads "A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz." So 4 W and 25 mW per 3 kHz stand whichever of the two instruments is in force on 17 November 2026.

---

## 5. Numeric consistency check

Every figure stated above was checked against every limit stated above:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| 4 W expressed in dBm | 36.02 dBm — matches 4000 mW, no rounding drift |
| 25 mW expressed in dBm | 13.98 dBm — matches 25 mW |
| Crossover bandwidth by linear ratio | 4000/25 × 3 kHz = 480 kHz |
| Crossover bandwidth by dB | (36.02 − 13.98) dB = 22.04 dB → ×160 → 480 kHz — agrees |
| Any table row exceeding 4 W EIRP? | No; the two wideband rows are explicitly capped at 4 W |
| Any table row exceeding 25 mW/3 kHz? | No; the 3 kHz row sits exactly at the limit |
| Per-MHz normalisation | 39.21 dBm/MHz — flagged illustrative, not substituted for the per-3 kHz limit |
| 10 mW (item 21) correctly excluded | Yes — identified as the general fallback row, not the digital-modulation row |
| 500 kHz minimum bandwidth correctly excluded | Yes — removed by Variation 2016 (No. 1), confirmed by its explanatory statement |

---

## 6. Deployment compliance checklist

For a digital-modulation transmitter intended to rely on item 59:

1. **Class fit** — confirm the device meets the licence's description of a *digital modulation transmitter*; check the licence dictionary before relying on the row.
2. **Frequency** — every emitted frequency strictly above 2400 MHz and at or below 2483.5 MHz, including occupied bandwidth edges, not just the carrier.
3. **Total radiated power** — worst-case EIRP in any direction ≤ 4 W (36.0 dBm), antenna gain included, across all power settings, modes and regulatory domains the hardware can be driven into.
4. **Radiated peak PSD** — worst-case 3 kHz slice anywhere in the emission ≤ 25 mW (13.98 dBm), measured radiated with a peak detector. Test at maximum power, all modulations and all bandwidth modes.
5. **Spectral regrowth** — verify PSD compliance at the emission shoulders and under any power-boost or beamforming mode; a compliant total power does not imply a compliant 3 kHz slice.
6. **Out-of-band and spurious emissions** — item 59's column 4 is silent on these; the licence's general conditions and the applicable ACMA EMC/spurious-emission requirements still apply and should be tested separately.
7. **Site conditions** — check the licence's general Part 2 conditions (including any site-based restrictions such as radio-astronomy locations) against the actual deployment coordinates before commissioning.
8. **Version control** — record which instrument and compilation the compliance file cites (currently F2015L01438 as amended, compilation F2023C00524), and re-baseline if the 2025 remake commences; the two numeric limits will not move, but the item and clause numbering will (item 59 / column 4 becomes item 7 / clause 43).

---

## 7. Sources relied on

- *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015*, compilation F2023C00524 registered 29 June 2023 — Schedule 1 items 21, 59; dictionary definition of *maximum EIRP*.
- Same instrument, compilation dated 17 April 2021 — items 21, 59; dictionary; conditions of operation.
- Same instrument, as made (F2015L01438, 15 September 2015) — items 21, 59 with the original limitation (b).
- *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence Variation 2016 (No. 1)* (F2016L00636) and its explanatory statement — removal of the 500 kHz minimum-bandwidth limitation from item 59.
- ACMA, *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025*, DRAFT FOR CONSULTATION (March 2025) — Schedule 1 item 7 and clause 43, used only to show the figures are unchanged by the pending remake.

# NASA-STD-4003A Class R (EMI/RF) Bonding - What the Standard Actually Requires

## 1. Direct answer to the two questions

**Q1. What maximum RF impedance, in ohms at a stated frequency, does NASA-STD-4003A allow across a Class R bond joint?**

**None. NASA-STD-4003A specifies no maximum RF impedance, in ohms or in any other unit, at any stated frequency, for a Class R bond joint.** The Class R clause (4.1.4) contains four requirements, and not one of them is an ohm-valued impedance limit at a frequency. Class R is a *performance* requirement: the path must be low enough in impedance (and inductance, including resonances) that interference does not occur at the frequencies of interest. The only number in the clause is a **dc** resistance limit of **2.5 milliohms per joint**, and the standard explicitly states that this number is *not* an RF criterion.

The nearest thing to a magnitude in the document is advisory text in the appendix, not a requirement:

> "The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration." (NASA-STD-4003A, App. B.3.4)

> "Any electronic equipment with conductive mounting feet will probably have an inductive reactance greater than 2.5 milliohms at frequencies above 10 megahertz (MHz). RF bonds may be satisfactory with several ohms of impedance; but, when straps are used, even these levels will be..." (App. B.3.4)

> "There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent." (App. B.3.4)

So a designer who asks "what ohm limit do I have to hit at 100 MHz?" will not find an answer in 4003A, because 4003A deliberately does not give one. The correct answer to give that designer is: *the standard requires you to show, by analysis, that the impedance of your specific bond configuration is low enough at your specific frequencies of interest; 2.5 milliohms dc per joint is a workmanship/consistency screen, not an RF acceptance value.*

**Q2. What does the standard actually require for a Class R joint?**

Clause 4.1.4, verbatim (Change 1 / revalidated text, EBR tags as issued):

> **4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)**
> The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.
>
> a. **[EBR 20]** All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.
>
> b. **[EBR 21]** All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.
>
> (1) **[EBR 22]** The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.
>
> c. **[EBR 23]** The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.

Requirement summary table (this is the deliverable answer to Q2):

| Req. | Type | Numeric limit | What it means for the joint |
|---|---|---|---|
| EBR 20 | Method | none | Bond per section 5.1 methods; path from equipment enclosure to structure |
| EBR 21 | Performance | **none** | Inductance *and* overall impedance, *including resonances*, low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest. This is the RF requirement, and it is verified by analysis, not by a number in the standard |
| EBR 22 | Numeric | **2.5 milliohms dc, per joint** (not per path) | dc resistance across *each joint* in the path |
| EBR 23 | Configuration | none | OML components Class R bonded to form a uniform low-impedance enclosure |

Supporting Class R characteristics from the standard's bonding-class table:

> "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort."
> "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required."
> FREQ. REQMT.: **High**. CURRENT REQMT.: **Low**.

And the related hardware rules that apply to a Class R joint: EBR 75 (bolt-count/low-impedance analysis where bolts are in the bond path), EBR 76 (fasteners sealed against moisture and air), EBR 77 (self-tapping screws, zinc-plated bolts/nuts/screws, star/anodized/zinc-plated washers, and cadmium-plated hardware shall not be used for bonding).

## 2. Why "2.5 milliohms" must not be quoted as the RF answer

A designer who answers the RF question with "2.5 milliohms" produces a noncompliant design review. The standard says so itself:

> "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond." (App. B.3.4)

> "The actual requirement is a maximum resistance of the Class R bond of 2.5 milliohms. However, this requirement can be met through a junction which has high impedance to the RF noise. The best assurance beyond the resistance measurement is review of the installation drawings for proper process specification call-outs and inspection of the actual installation." (NASA EMC guidance, NTRS 19970005154, C.2.3.5.2)

Mechanism, from the standard's own equivalent circuit: the bond is R in series with L, in parallel with C. Below the frequency where wL = R the impedance is the dc resistance; above it, impedance rises at 20 dB/decade until parallel resonance, where "the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q)... The Q is high when the resistance is low, which is usually the case for a bonding joint." That is precisely why EBR 21 says "including resonances" and why a dc milliohmmeter reading cannot close a Class R requirement.

## 3. Procedure a designer should actually follow (since 4003A gives no ohm limit)

Because EBR 21 is performance-based, the impedance limit must come from the *program*, not from 4003A. Do this:

**Step 1 - Get the frequency-of-interest set.** From the vehicle EMC control plan / MIL-STD-464 tailoring, list the frequencies at which the bond carries RF return current (e.g., transmitter fundamentals and harmonics, clock harmonics, shield-termination return currents, lightning/EMP spectrum if applicable). EBR 21 is evaluated at *these* frequencies, not at a generic one.

**Step 2 - Derive a project Z_max(f).** The number is set by whatever the bond must support: shield termination effectiveness, filter return impedance, or an enclosure transfer-impedance budget allocated in the EMC plan. Record it as a program requirement (e.g., "|Z_bond| <= Z_max(f) at each f_i"), citing the EMC plan, *not* NASA-STD-4003A. Do not write "per NASA-STD-4003A" next to an ohm value; that is the error this memo exists to prevent.

**Step 3 - Compute the bond path impedance.** For a strap of length l, width w, thickness t (all in cm):

  L (nH) = 2*l*[ ln( 2*l / (w + t) ) + 0.5 + 0.2235*(w + t)/l ]

  R_ac = R_dc * (1 + skin-effect correction) ~ R_dc for f below a few MHz on typical strap thicknesses; above that R_ac grows as sqrt(f) but is normally still small versus wL.

  Z(f) = sqrt( R_ac^2 + (2*pi*f*L)^2 ), evaluated at each f_i, and checked for parallel resonance with the local C (case-to-structure capacitance, strap-over-structure capacitance).

**Worked example (illustration only - not a standard value).** 10 cm long x 2 cm wide x 1 mm thick copper strap:
  l = 10, w + t = 2.1; L = 2*10*[ln(20/2.1) + 0.5 + 0.2235*0.21] = 20*[2.254 + 0.5 + 0.0469] = **56.0 nH**.
  - Crossover where wL = 2.5 milliohms: f = R/(2*pi*L) = 0.0025/(2*pi*56e-9) = **7.1 kHz**. Above ~7 kHz the dc requirement is irrelevant to RF performance.
  - |Z| at 10 MHz = 2*pi*1e7*56e-9 = **3.5 ohm**.
  - |Z| at 100 MHz = **35 ohm**.
  Shortening the same-width strap to 5 cm gives L = 2*5*[ln(10/2.1) + 0.5 + 0.2235*0.42] = 10*[1.561 + 0.5 + 0.0939] = **21.5 nH**, i.e. |Z| = 13.5 ohm at 100 MHz. Length is the dominant lever; this is the quantitative reason behind the standard's "short, wide strap" language and the widely used l/w <= 5 strap rule.

**Step 4 - Design to the computed number.** In priority order per the standard's Class R table: direct metal-to-metal faying-surface contact (preferred, no jumper); if a strap is unavoidable, make it short and wide (l/w <= 5), thin, and use multiple parallel straps to divide inductance; never route the bond through an adjacent part; keep isolated elements well away from quarter-wavelength dimensions at the frequencies of interest.

**Step 5 - Verify and document.**
  - dc: 4-wire Kelvin measurement across *each joint*, <= 2.5 milliohms (EBR 22), after the specified surface preparation and with the specified hardware (EBR 76/77).
  - RF: analysis, not measurement - "it is usually impractical to measure inductance" (App. B.3.4). Submit the Z(f) calculation against the project Z_max(f), with resonance check, as the EBR 21 compliance evidence.
  - If bolts are in the path: bolt-count/low-impedance analysis per EBR 75.

**Step 6 - Drawing note template.** State the standard's requirement and the program's derived limit separately, so the two are never confused:

  "BOND PER NASA-STD-4003, CLASS R. DC RESISTANCE ACROSS EACH JOINT SHALL NOT EXCEED 2.5 MILLIOHMS (EBR 22). BOND PATH INDUCTANCE SHALL NOT EXCEED ___ nH AND |Z| SHALL NOT EXCEED ___ OHMS AT ___ MHz, PER EMC CONTROL PLAN ___ (SATISFIES EBR 21). DIRECT METAL-TO-METAL CONTACT REQUIRED; NO JUMPERS. USE NO SELF-TAPPING SCREWS, ZINC-PLATED OR CADMIUM-PLATED HARDWARE, OR STAR/ANODIZED WASHERS (EBR 77). SEAL FASTENERS (EBR 76)."

## 4. Scope caveat worth passing to the designer

Class R is not required on every item; the standard notes it is "difficult to determine in advance which equipment really needs to be well bonded," and that the low impedance to structure matters specifically for power-line-to-chassis filters and for cable shields terminated to the chassis. Apply Class R where the EMC plan shows RF return current, and do not spend mass and cost chasing 2.5 milliohms on hardware whose RF impedance is inductance-dominated anyway.

## 5. Bottom line

- Maximum RF impedance allowed by NASA-STD-4003A across a Class R joint, in ohms at any frequency: **none is specified**. The requirement is performance-based (EBR 21).
- The only numeric Class R requirement: **dc resistance across each joint <= 2.5 milliohms** (EBR 22), which the standard itself says is not an RF criterion.
- The ohm-valued limit a design must meet comes from the program EMC/EMI control plan, derived and verified by impedance-vs-frequency analysis of the actual bond path, including resonances.

answer:
## Ask 1 — Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP: **60 °C/W**

**Source:** Microchip ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/328P complete datasheet, **DS40002061B (09/2020)**, Section **37.9 "Thermal Specifications"**, **Table 37-9**:

| Symbol | Description | Typ. | Unit | Conditions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **θJA** | **Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient** | **60** | **°C/W** | **28-pin PDIP package (SP)** |
| θJA | Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient | 47 | °C/W | 28-pin SOIC package (SO) |
| θJA | Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient | 67.1 | °C/W | 28-pin SSOP package (SS) |
| θJA | Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient | 36.1 | °C/W | 32-pin VQFN package (RXB) |
| θJA | Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient | 58.8 | °C/W | 32-pin TQFP package (PT) |

Notes on this number:

- The 60 °C/W figure is a **typical** value. The table publishes no maximum, no spread and no airflow/test-board qualifier beyond the package designator; it is the still-air, JEDEC-style package number, not a guaranteed worst case.
- "SP" is the 28-lead, 0.300"-wide PDIP (package drawing 28P3). The matching order codes are **ATmega328P-PU** (industrial, −40 °C to 85 °C) and **ATmega328P-PN** (industrial, −40 °C to 105 °C).
- If the design moves off the PDIP, the same table's other rows apply; do not carry 60 °C/W over to a TQFP or VQFN layout.

## Ask 2 — Maximum junction temperature / total power dissipation: **no numeric value is specified in the thermal table**

In Table 37-9 the second row reads, verbatim:

> **TJMAX — Maximum Junction Temperature — Refer to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section**

That is the entire entry. The table does **not** publish a numeric TJ,max, and it does **not** publish a numeric PD,max. The only quantitative content in the table's notes is the *method*, not a limit:

- **Device dissipation:** `PDIS = VCC × (IDD − Σ IOH) + Σ {(VCC − VOH) × IOH} + Σ (VOL × IOL)`
- **Internal dissipation:** `PINTERNAL = IDD × VCC` (IDD = chip current with no output loading)
- **Derated power:** printed as `PDER = PDMAX (TJ − TA)/θJA`; dimensionally this must be read as the allowable dissipation for a given junction-to-ambient rise, i.e. `PDER = (TJ − TA)/θJA`, with PDMAX being whatever ceiling the Absolute Maximum Ratings section imposes at TJ.

Consequences for the design file:

1. **Do not write "TJ,max = 150 °C" or "PD,max = 1 W" into the requirements as a datasheet fact.** Neither appears in Table 37-9. 150 °C is a common AVR-family assumption, not a quoted DS40002061B thermal-table value; if it is adopted it must be labelled an *assumption* and either confirmed in writing by Microchip or replaced by the Absolute Maximum Ratings entry.
2. **The hard ambient limit is set by the order code**, from the ordering-information table: −40 °C to **85 °C** for ATmega328P-PU, −40 °C to **105 °C** for ATmega328P-PN. That is the only temperature ceiling the datasheet states numerically for normal operation.
3. **The usable design equation is therefore:** `TJ = TA + PD × θJA`, with θJA = 60 °C/W for the 28-pin PDIP and TA ≤ 85 °C (-PU) or ≤ 105 °C (-PN). Keep the computed TJ below whatever TJ,max the Absolute Maximum Ratings section (or Microchip support) confirms; until that is confirmed, treat the junction limit as an open item in the thermal budget rather than a datasheet number.

### Worked check (arithmetic re-verified)

- PD = 0.15 W (5 V, ~30 mA total with light I/O loading), TA = 85 °C:  
  `TJ = 85 + 0.15 × 60 = 85 + 9 = 94 °C`.  
  Rise is 9 °C; no stated limit is crossed.
- PD = 1.00 W, TA = 85 °C: `TJ = 85 + 60 = 145 °C` — this already exceeds any plausible 125 °C-class limit and is inside a 150 °C limit only by 5 °C. The PDIP alone gives no margin at 1 W.
- For reference only (assumption, not a datasheet value): if a 150 °C junction limit were adopted, the ceiling at 85 °C ambient would be `(150 − 85)/60 = 1.083 W`. Label this "assumed TJ,max" wherever it is used.

### Layout / enclosure guidance that follows from the 60 °C/W figure

- 60 °C/W is a still-air, unbounded package number. A socketed PDIP inside a sealed enclosure, with no copper spreading and no venting, will run materially hotter; for first-pass budgeting use 1.5–2× (90–120 °C/W effective) and confirm by thermocouple on the package top at worst-case ambient.
- PDIP leads are the only heat path. Solder all 28 leads (including the ground and VCC pins) to copper; a 2-layer board with 1 oz copper and a ground pour under the part is the minimum. A socket adds a real interface resistance — avoid ZIF/socket in hot enclosures.
- Keep the crystal/resonator and the AREF/AVCC filter away from the package's thermal plume if the ADC is used near the 85 °C corner.

### What the answer depends on

- Datasheet revision: older 8271-series (2012/2013) summaries do not carry Table 37-9 at all; the 60 °C/W figure is the DS40002061B number.
- Package: any move to 32-pin TQFP (58.8 °C/W) or VQFN (36.1 °C/W) changes both θJA and the assembly/thermal path; the 60 °C/W figure applies only to the 28P3 PDIP.
- Order code: -PU vs -PN changes the ambient ceiling (85 vs 105 °C) and therefore the allowable PD at a fixed TJ.
