question: X19
answer:
ANSWER

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (and Rev. 5.1) control AC-7 does not require any specific number of attempts, time period, or lockout duration. All three are organization-defined assignment parameters. There is no numeric answer in the control, and no numeric answer anywhere in AC-7's discussion or enhancements. The requirement AC-7 actually imposes is procedural: the organization must (a) choose and document a number and a counting window, and (b) choose and document at least one automatic response when the limit is exceeded, including a duration only if the timed-lockout option is the one selected.

| Ask | What AC-7 actually says | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | AC-7a: `[Assignment: organization-defined number]` | Organization-defined. No NIST value. |
| 2. Time period | AC-7a: `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` | Organization-defined. No NIST value. |
| 3. Lockout duration | AC-7b: `lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]` — one option in a Selection | Organization-defined, and conditional: no duration parameter exists if a different Selection option is chosen. |

VERBATIM CONTROL TEXT (identical in the primary Rev. 5 PDF, sha256 fc63bcd61715, and the OSCAL-derived Rev. 5.1 PDF, sha256 9ce01f4d67c9)

AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS

Control:
a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

Discussion: The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period. If a delay algorithm is selected, organizations may employ different algorithms for different components of the system based on the capabilities of those components. Responses to unsuccessful logon attempts may be implemented at the operating system and the application levels. [Discussion continues: organization-defined actions may include a secret question in addition to username/password, lockdown mode with limited capabilities instead of full lockout, logon restricted to specified IP addresses, CAPTCHA, or user profiles based on location/time/IP/device/MAC; if automatic lockout or a delay algorithm is not implemented in support of availability, organizations consider a combination of other actions; users can be prompted with a secret question before the limit is exceeded; and — from the CTID reproduction, see provenance note — "Automatically unlocking an account after a specified period of time is generally not permitted. However, exceptions may be required based on operational mission or need."]

PARAMETER INVENTORY — the complete list of values AC-7 requires an organization to supply

| ID | Parameter | Location | Type | Value supplied by NIST? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | AC-7a | Assignment | No |
| P2 | Time period over which consecutive invalid attempts are counted | AC-7a | Assignment | No |
| P3 | Lockout duration | AC-7b, option 1 | Assignment, conditional on Selection | No |
| P4 | Delay algorithm | AC-7b, option 3 | Assignment, conditional on Selection | No |
| P5 | Other action | AC-7b, option 5 | Assignment, conditional on Selection | No |
| P6 | Number of consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts before purge/wipe | AC-7(2) | Assignment | No |
| P7 | Number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts | AC-7(3) | Assignment | No |
| P8 | Alternate authentication factors permitted after lockout | AC-7(4)(a) | Assignment | No |
| P9 | Number of consecutive invalid attempts via alternate factors, and the time period | AC-7(4)(b) | Assignment (two) | No |

WHY ASK 3 IS STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT FROM ASKS 1 AND 2

P1 and P2 are unconditional: every AC-7 implementation must have a number and a window, because part (a) has no alternatives. P3 is not. Part (b) is a `Selection (one or more)`. If the organization selects 'lock the account or node until released by an administrator,' there is no duration parameter at all and the lock persists indefinitely until an administrator acts. If it selects the delay algorithm, P4 replaces a lockout. If it selects 'notify system administrator' or 'take other action,' the account may never be locked. So 'what lockout duration does AC-7 require' has no answer even at the parameter level until the organization makes its Selection — the question of a duration may not arise.

There is also a genuine tension inside the Discussion that the organization must resolve in its SSP rather than assume away: the text says automatic lockouts 'are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period,' and later says 'Automatically unlocking an account after a specified period of time is generally not permitted. However, exceptions may be required based on operational mission or need.' A timed lockout (P3) is contemplated by part (b) and by the first sentence, while the second sentence pushes toward administrator release. Document the choice and the operational justification either way.

WHAT IS NOT THE SOURCE OF ANY NUMBER

No fetched passage — the primary Rev. 5 PDF, the Rev. 5.1 OSCAL-derived PDF, the GitHub wiki mirror, or the CTID mapping page — contains a numeric value for attempts, window, or lockout duration. Any specific figures you have seen attributed to AC-7 (three attempts, fifteen minutes, thirty minutes, and similar) are one of: an organization's own assignment recorded in its SSP or policy; a value assigned by an overlay, baseline, or authorization program; or a misattribution. They are not in the AC-7 text. I did not fetch SP 800-53B and therefore make no claim about whether it assigns AC-7 parameters; that is outside the evidence I hold.

HOW TO CLOSE THIS OUT FOR A REAL SYSTEM

1. Record P1 and P2 as explicit values in the SSP control implementation statement for AC-7a, with rationale tied to the system's threat environment (brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying are the techniques the CTID mapping associates with AC-7).
2. Record the AC-7b Selection (one or more options) and, only if the timed-lock option is chosen, P3.
3. If AC-7(4) is implemented, record P8 and P9 so the alternate-factor path does not become a bypass of the primary limit.
4. Assess against the documented values, not against a NIST figure — there is none to assess against. An assessor can only find AC-7 unsatisfied if the organization has not defined the values or the system does not enforce the values the organization defined.

EXAMPLE ORGANIZATIONAL ASSIGNMENT — NOT A NIST REQUIREMENT, NOT VERIFIED AGAINST ANY SOURCE

If your program needs a defensible starting point, a common pattern is: 3 to 5 consecutive invalid attempts counted within a 15-minute window, with a 30-minute timed lockout or release by an administrator, plus AC-7(4) alternate-factor recovery to limit denial of service. These are three independent parameters; the 30-minute lock being longer than the 15-minute counting window is not a conflict, since the counter resets on successful logon and the window governs counting, not lock length. This paragraph is engineering guidance from the author of this document, not a quotation, and must be recorded as your organization's assignment if adopted.

PROVENANCE AND CONFIDENCE

- Control text: high confidence. Two independent NIST-published renderings (primary PDF, OSCAL-derived PDF) and a third-party mirror agree character-for-character on AC-7a and AC-7b.
- Discussion, through the sentence about delay algorithms: high confidence (primary PDF).
- Discussion, final sentences including 'Automatically unlocking an account after a specified period of time is generally not permitted': medium-high confidence. Captured from the CTID reproduction (sha256 47ef8c325aa1) because the primary PDF excerpt was truncated mid-Discussion. Verify against the PDF before quoting in an authorization package.
- The draft markup PDF (sha256 8574eeabc495) is an earlier Rev. 5 draft, not the final publication; its AC-7 differs (no 'notify system administrator' option, hyphenated 'time-period'). It is cited here only as corroboration that the parameter-driven structure was stable, not as authority.

# Compliance determination — LIPD Class Licence, 'digital modulation' transmitter, 2400–2483.5 MHz, as at 17 November 2026

## 1. Determination

| Ask | Question | Determination |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Maximum EIRP for a digital modulation transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz | **4 W** (36.0 dBm) |
| 4 | Additional limitation on radiated peak power spectral density | **25 mW per 3 kHz** (13.98 dBm per 3 kHz; 8.33 mW per kHz) |
| 5 | Year carried in the name of the instrument in force on 17 Nov 2026 | **2025** — *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025* (F2025L01047) |

## 2. Governing instrument (basis for ask 5)

The instrument in force on 17 November 2026 is the **Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025** (F2025L01047), because:

- It was made by the ACMA under s 132 of the *Radiocommunications Act 1992*, dated **4 September 2025** (signatures of Adam Suckling and Michael Brealey).
- It was registered on the Federal Register of Legislation on **5 September 2025** ("Authorised Version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025").
- Clause 2 (Commencement): "This instrument commences at the start of 1 October 2025."

1 October 2025 precedes 17 November 2026, and no later instrument or variation appears in the material retrieved, so the 2025 instrument is the operative text on the date in question and the year in its name is **2025**.

Predecessors are expressly **not** the instrument in force on that date and are used here only as corroboration:

- *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015* (F2015L01438, as amended — compilation F2023C00524);
- *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2000* (compilation F2014C00930 / F2005B00339).

## 3. Maximum EIRP (basis for ask 2)

Schedule 1 of the 2025 instrument, table of classes of radiocommunications transmitters, item 7, quoted verbatim:

> "7 Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43"

Column 3 is the **Maximum EIRP** column. Therefore the maximum EIRP for a digital modulation transmitter operating in 2400–2483.5 MHz is **4 W = 36.0 dBm = 4000 mW**.

Two points of construction that matter to the determination:

1. Item 7 carries **no averaging qualifier**. Compare items 8 and 10 in the same table, which read "1 W, averaged over the entire transmission burst" and "200 mW, averaged over the entire transmission burst". The absence of that qualifier on item 7 means the 4 W cap is not burst-averaged; it is the maximum (peak) EIRP radiated in any direction.
2. The neighbouring entry "Any 2400–2483.5 MHz 10 mW None" is a **separate, lower-power general authorisation** for devices that do not meet a class-specific item. It is an alternative route to authorisation, not a constraint that reduces the 4 W available to a device that satisfies item 7 and clause 43.

## 4. Additional limitation on radiated peak power spectral density (basis for ask 4)

Column 4 of item 7 reads "See clause 43". Section 4 of the 2025 instrument defines the term used by that column:

> "**additional limitation**, for a class of radiocommunications transmitters, means a limitation in a clause mentioned in column 4 of the table item in Schedule 1 for that class."

So the "additional limit" asked about is the content of **clause 43**. Clause 43 is the single clause serving all three digital-modulation items (915–928 MHz, 2400–2483.5 MHz and 5725–5850 MHz), and the condition attaching to the digital modulation class in this band is the long-standing spectral-density condition:

> **The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz.**

Provenance for that wording (three independent sources, all in the retrieved material):

- 2015 instrument, Schedule 1 item 59 — "Digital modulation transmitters | 2400–2483.5 | 4 W | The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz."
- 2000 instrument, Schedule 1 item 45A — "Digital modulation transmitters | 2400–2483.5 | 4 W | 1. The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz is limited to 25 mW per 3 kHz."
- ACMA's published summary of 2.4 GHz authorisations — "59 Digital modulation transmitters | 2400–2483.5 | 4 W | The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz must not exceed 25 mW per 3 kHz."

The identical condition applied to all three DM items in the predecessor instruments, which is consistent with the 2025 instrument consolidating them behind one clause (43).

**Verification step before sign-off (mandatory):** read clause 43 verbatim in the compiled F2025L01047 on the Federal Register. The clause text itself was not reproduced in the retrieved passages; the value above is carried from the identical condition on the same class and band in both predecessor instruments and in the regulator's own summary. If the words of clause 43 differ in any respect (different resolution bandwidth, different power, or an added bandwidth/technology condition), **clause 43 governs** and this determination is to be reissued with the clause text quoted.

## 5. Units, conversions and internal consistency check

| Quantity | Value | Equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum EIRP | 4 W | 36.0 dBm; 4000 mW; ≈ 2.44 W ERP (33.85 dBm ERP) |
| Radiated peak PSD | 25 mW per 3 kHz | 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz; 8.33 mW per kHz; ≈ 15.2 mW per 3 kHz ERP |

Consistency of the two limits with each other (they must not contradict): 4 W spread across a 500 kHz emission is 8 mW/kHz, i.e. **24 mW in any 3 kHz, which is within the 25 mW per 3 kHz cap**. The two numbers are therefore mutually compatible. Conversely, the narrowest emission that can carry the full 4 W while staying inside the PSD cap is 4 W ÷ 25 mW × 3 kHz = **480 kHz** — which is exactly why the predecessor instruments paired the 4 W / 25 mW per 3 kHz limits with a "minimum 6 dB bandwidth of at least 500 kHz" condition.

Practical consequence for a device narrower than ~480 kHz: the PSD cap binds, and permitted EIRP reduces to 25 mW per 3 kHz × (emission bandwidth ÷ 3 kHz). For example, a 100 kHz-wide emission is limited to ≈ 833 mW EIRP, not 4 W.

## 6. How to apply the determination (compliance test procedure)

1. **Class check.** Confirm the device is a *digital modulation* radiocommunications transmitter within the meaning of s 4 of the 2025 instrument — i.e. an intentional radiator using digital modulation, not a frequency-hopping transmitter (items 2/3), not an RLAN (items 10 et seq.), and not a wireless microphone/audio device (Schedule 1 Part 2). A device that fits a different class takes that class's limits.
2. **Band check.** Confirm operation lies wholly within 2400–2483.5 MHz. In the LIPD tables the lower limit is exclusive and the upper limit inclusive, so 2400 MHz exactly is outside and 2483.5 MHz exactly is inside; keep a margin for occupied bandwidth and frequency tolerance.
3. **EIRP test.** Measure maximum EIRP in any direction under worst-case modulation and highest power setting: must be **≤ 36.0 dBm (4 W)**. Not burst-averaged for this item.
4. **PSD test.** Measure radiated peak power spectral density with a 3 kHz resolution bandwidth, worst case anywhere in the emission and across all modulation/power states: must be **≤ 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz (25 mW per 3 kHz)**.
5. **Both conditions apply simultaneously.** Meeting the 4 W EIRP cap does not discharge the PSD condition, and vice versa. Record the measurement bandwidth and detector used, since the limit is defined in a 3 kHz reference bandwidth.
6. **Other obligations.** Operation remains subject to the general conditions of the 2025 instrument (Part 1/Part 2), and to the prohibition on causing interference. Band-edge and out-of-band emission limits are outside the scope of this determination and must be checked against the relevant clause before sign-off.

## 7. Scope notes

- The instrument states **EIRP**; do not report ERP as if it were the limit. If ERP is needed for a datasheet, the conversion is −2.15 dB (4 W EIRP ≈ 2.44 W ERP; 25 mW/3 kHz EIRP ≈ 15.2 mW/3 kHz ERP).
- The determination is made against the text of F2025L01047 as registered 5 September 2025 and commencing 1 October 2025. If a variation commences between that date and 17 November 2026, the varied text governs; re-check the version in force on the date before relying on these figures.
- This is a compliance determination on power limits only. It is not legal advice, and it does not address EMC, electrical safety, health/EME exposure or spectrum-licensing obligations that may apply to a product independently of the class licence.

ANSWER TO THE DESIGNER'S QUESTION

NASA-STD-4003A (Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment), including Change 1 and the 2026 revalidated edition, does NOT specify a maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency across a Class R bond joint. The question's premise is incorrect. If you write an ohm value at a frequency on a drawing and attribute it to NASA-STD-4003A, you are citing a requirement that does not exist in that document.

WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY REQUIRES FOR CLASS R (Section 4.1.4)

Intent statement: 'The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies.'

- [EBR 20] All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.
- [EBR 21] All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.  <-- This is the RF requirement. It is qualitative. No ohms, no frequency, no test method.
- [EBR 22] The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.  <-- This is the ONLY numeric limit in the Class R clause. It is a dc resistance, not an RF impedance.
- [EBR 23] The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.
- [EBR 24] Hatches, access panels, doors, and other apertures in outer mold line components shall have at minimum a Class R electrical bond to the outer mold line material.

Related 2.5-milliohm figures elsewhere in the same standard (all dc, none RF): backshell-to-case path (EBR 27); antenna return paths on metallic and composite OML surfaces; joints in paths expected to carry high-amplitude lightning current (EBR 30/EBR 33).

TABLE 1 (SUMMARY OF BONDING CLASSES), CLASS R COLUMN
- DC bond resistance requirement: 'Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.'
- Frequency requirement: High.
- Current requirement: Low.
- Narrative: 'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.'
Note that even Table 1, the most quotable summary in the document, states no ohm value and no frequency.

WHY THERE IS NO OHM/FREQUENCY NUMBER (Appendix B.3.4 rationale, verbatim in substance)
- 'There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent.'
- 'The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest.'
- The value depends on surface preparation (conversion coating chemistry and thickness), faying-surface contact area, and contact pressure.
- 'The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration.'
- 'One should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms... Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest.'
- Isolated structural elements approaching 1/4 wavelength can pick up and re-radiate RF or arc; this must be considered when sizing Class R straps or jumpers.

So the standard deliberately declines to set an RF impedance limit. It sets a dc screening limit (2.5 milliohms per joint) and pushes the actual RF performance obligation onto the designer as an analysis obligation at the program's frequencies of interest.

HOW TO SATISFY EBR 21 IN PRACTICE (designer's method, since the standard gives no number)

1. Establish the frequencies of interest from the program EMI/EMC control plan (e.g., the emissions/susceptibility bands actually specified, commonly 30 MHz to 1 GHz or 18 GHz, plus any transmitter fundamental/harmonic). Record them; they become the 'stated frequencies' your analysis uses. The standard will not supply them.
2. Model the joint and the whole path as R + jwL (add resonance terms only if the path length approaches a quarter wavelength at the highest frequency of interest). Use Z(f) = sqrt(R_dc^2 + (2*pi*f*L)^2).
3. Compute L from the actual geometry. For a rectangular strap, a standard closed form is L (uH) = 0.002 * l * [ ln( 2l / (w + t) ) + 0.5 + 0.2235 * (w + t) / l ], with l, w, t in cm.
   Worked example: copper strap, l = 10 cm, w = 1.27 cm, t = 0.05 cm -> L = 0.002 * 10 * [ ln(20/1.32) + 0.5 + 0.2235*1.32/10 ] = 0.002 * 10 * [2.718 + 0.5 + 0.0295] = 0.0649 uH, i.e. about 65 nH.
   With R_dc = 2.5 milliohms: |Z| at 1 MHz = 0.41 ohm; at 10 MHz = 4.1 ohm; at 100 MHz = 40.8 ohm; at 400 MHz = 163 ohm.
   Crossover where X_L equals the 2.5-milliohm dc limit: f = 0.0025 / (2*pi*65e-9) = about 6.1 kHz. Above roughly 6 kHz the dc resistance is no longer the controlling term for that geometry. This is exactly the point Appendix B.3.4 makes, and it is why an 'ohms at a frequency' limit would have to be geometry-specific to be meaningful.
4. Reduce L rather than chase dc milliohms once you are above that crossover: shorten the path, widen it, use direct metal-to-metal faying contact over large area, avoid jumpers, avoid strap runs approaching a quarter wavelength at the highest frequency of interest.
5. Document the result as an analysis in the bonding/EMI compliance report. EBR 21 is verified by analysis and inspection, not by an ohm-meter pass/fail, because the standard itself notes that 'it is usually impractical to measure inductance or current carrying capability' on flight hardware.
6. Verify EBR 22 by measurement: four-wire (Kelvin) bond-resistance measurement across each joint in the path, 2.5 milliohms maximum per joint, recorded per joint, not per path.

WHAT TO PUT ON THE DRAWING OR ICD
Write both halves, and do not invent a third:
'Class R electrical bond per NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, para. 4.1.4. DC resistance across each joint in the bond path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms (EBR 22). Bond path inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, shall be shown by analysis to be low enough to prevent interference over the program frequencies of interest (EBR 21) — [insert program-defined band, e.g., 30 MHz to 1 GHz]. Direct metal-to-metal contact preferred; no jumpers; short, wide strap only as last resort.'
If your program needs a hard RF number (transfer impedance, surface transfer impedance, or maximum bond impedance in ohms at a frequency), it must come from a program-level document, an EMI/EMC control plan, or a cited standard such as MIL-STD-464 or SAE ARP 1481 — not from NASA-STD-4003A. NASA-STD-4003A is the base bonding standard and permits tailoring by contract or program specification; that tailoring is where any ohm/frequency limit would legally live.

SCOPE CAVEATS
- The clause applies 'across each joint in the path,' not per fastener, not per unit area, and not to the whole path summed. Do not convert it to a per-fastener allocation unless your program document says so.
- Class R is not required on all equipment; the standard notes it is difficult to predict which equipment needs it, but low impedance to structure is needed for power-line-to-chassis filters and for cable shields terminated to chassis.
- Revision basis: the Class R text quoted above is identical in NASA-STD-4003A, NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, and the 2026 revalidated edition; the 2003 predecessor NASA-STD-4003 likewise set 2.5 milliohms dc and no RF ohm limit. The answer is therefore revision-insensitive within the 4003 family.

question: X41
answer:
THERMAL DATA FOR THE ATmega328P, 28-PIN PDIP (28P3 / 0.300in body)

=== BOTTOM LINE ===
1) Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, 28-pin PDIP (SP / 28P3): theta-JA = 60 degC/W (typical, JEDEC-style still-air board measurement).
2) Maximum temperature specified: 125 degC. The ATmega328P Absolute Maximum Ratings give an operating temperature of -55 degC to +125 degC. There is NO separate TJ(max) parameter and NO tabulated Ptot parameter; total power dissipation must be derived as Ptot = (TJ - TA)/theta-JA.

=== ASK 1: SOURCE / REVISION CONTROL ===
Document: Microchip ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/328P data sheet, "Data Sheet Complete DS40002061B", (c) 2020 Microchip Technology Inc., 09/2020. This supersedes Atmel-8271J-AVR (10/2014). The electrical content of 8271J and DS40002061B is identical; only the branding/page footers changed. Verify page footers read "Data Sheet Complete DS40002061B-page NNN" on your copy.

=== WHAT DS40002061B ACTUALLY CONTAINS ON THERMAL (important caveat) ===
The ATmega328P Electrical Characteristics section (Absolute Maximum Ratings / DC Characteristics / Speed Grades / Clock, System-Reset, TWI, SPI, ADC characteristics) does NOT contain a "Thermal Characteristics" table. There is no theta-JA row, no theta-JC row, no TJ(max) parameter and no Ptot parameter anywhere in this data sheet. The Absolute Maximum Ratings list, in substance, only:
  - Operating Temperature ................... -55 degC to +125 degC
  - Storage Temperature ..................... -65 degC to +150 degC
  - Voltage on any pin except RESET vs GND ... -0.5 V to VCC+0.5 V
  - Voltage on RESET vs GND ................. -0.5 V to +13.0 V
  - Maximum Operating Voltage ............... 6.0 V
  - DC Current, VCC and GND pins ............ 200.0 mA
  - DC Current, any I/O pin ................. 40.0 mA
Consequence: the 60 degC/W figure below is Microchip's published thermal specification for the 28-pin PDIP (SP) package, not a line item inside DS40002061B. Quote it as "Microchip 28-pin PDIP (SP) package thermal specification" in a design review, NOT as "ATmega328P data sheet section 33". If your QA process requires a data-sheet-traceable number, the only honest statement is: not specified; use the package value with margin, or measure it (see Verification section).

=== ASK 2: theta-JA FOR THE 28-PIN PDIP ===
theta-JA = 60 degC/W (typical).
Provenance and corroboration:
  - Microchip thermal specification table, 28-pin PDIP package (SP): theta-JA = 60 degC/W.
  - Independent Microchip table for a 28-pin SPDIP package (PIC18F26K40 family): theta-JA = 60 degC/W.
  Two unrelated Microchip product families give the same 60 degC/W for the 28-pin, 0.300in PDIP/SPDIP outline, which is what makes 60 degC/W a defensible package-level value for the ATmega328P-PU / -PN (both order codes use package code 28P3).
Values found in the source material and why they are REJECTED for this part:
  - 48 degC/W "28-pin PDIP (SP)": that table also lists a 20-pin SSOP, a 28-pin SSOP and a 32-pin VQFN and belongs to a device with MVIO/DAC/ZCD peripherals (AVR-DA family). Wrong die, wrong pad geometry, wrong table.
  - TJMAX = 150 degC from the same PIC18F table: do NOT carry 150 degC across to the ATmega328P. The AVR absolute maximum is 125 degC.
Basis of the number: the value is a JEDEC 2S2P (four-layer, two power planes, no airflow, EIA/JESD 51-7) still-air board measurement, as stated in Microchip's companion thermal tables. It is a TYPICAL value only - Microchip publishes no maximum.

=== ASK 3: MAXIMUM JUNCTION TEMPERATURE / TOTAL POWER DISSIPATION ===
Maximum temperature specified: 125 degC (Absolute Maximum Ratings, "Operating Temperature -55 degC to +125 degC"). This is the die-temperature ceiling to use in the thermal calculation.
Do not confuse this with the qualified operating ranges, which are narrower:
  - ATmega328P-PU / -AU / -MU / -MMH (standard): -40 degC to +85 degC ambient
  - ATmega328P-PN / -AN / -MN (extended): -40 degC to +105 degC ambient
Guaranteed operation is only within those ranges; 125 degC is the damage/stress boundary, not an operating endorsement.
Total power dissipation: NOT specified in DS40002061B. Derive it.
  Ptot(max, TA) = (TJ(max) - TA) / theta-JA = (125 - TA)/60
  TA = 25 degC  -> 1.667 W
  TA = 40 degC  -> 1.417 W
  TA = 55 degC  -> 1.167 W
  TA = 70 degC  -> 0.917 W
  TA = 85 degC  -> 0.667 W   (the -PU/-AU rating point)
  TA = 105 degC -> 0.333 W   (the -PN/-AN rating point)
Binding limit check (this is where the thermal number and the absolute-max current limit interact):
  The VCC/GND pin current limit is 200 mA absolute maximum. At VCC = 5.5 V that is 1.10 W. 1.10 W x 60 degC/W = 66 degC rise, so TJ reaches 125 degC at TA = 59 degC.
  Therefore: below ~59 degC ambient the 200 mA current limit binds before the thermal limit (1.10 W < 1.667 W at 25 degC); above ~59 degC the thermal derating binds. Neither figure ever exceeds a limit set elsewhere in this document.

=== POWER MODEL (from the data sheet's own dissipation notes) ===
  Pdis = VDD x (IDD - sum IOH) + sum[(VDD - VOH) x IOH] + sum[VOL x IOL]
  Pinternal = IDD x VDD   (IDD = current to run the chip alone, no output loads)
  Derated power (Microchip's form): PDER = PDMAX x (TJ - TA)/theta-JA
  Self-heating: TJ = TA + Ptot x theta-JA

=== WORKED EXAMPLE: ATmega328P-PU, 5 V, 16 MHz, 85 degC ambient ===
  Internal: IDD ~ 15 mA typ -> 5 V x 15 mA = 75 mW
  I/O: 8 outputs sinking 10 mA each, VOL = 0.6 V -> 8 x 6 mW = 48 mW
  Ptot = 123 mW -> rise = 0.123 x 60 = 7.4 degC -> TJ = 92.4 degC at TA = 85 degC.
  Headroom to 125 degC: 32.6 degC = 0.54 W of additional dissipation. Comfortable.
  Stress case: full 200 mA through the I/O structure at an average 0.8 V drop (160 mW) plus 75 mW internal = 235 mW -> 14.1 degC rise -> TJ = 99 degC at 85 degC ambient. Still inside 125 degC.

=== DESIGN GUIDANCE FOR A REAL BOARD ===
  - 60 degC/W is a 2S2P JEDEC board number. A 28-pin PDIP in a socket, on a 2-layer board with no copper pour under the part and still air, behaves worse - budget 70 to 75 degC/W. At 75 degC/W and TA = 85 degC the allowable dissipation is (125-85)/75 = 0.533 W (vs 0.667 W at 60 degC/W).
  - Never place the PDIP where ambient exceeds the part's qualified range (85 degC for -PU, 105 degC for -PN) regardless of how low the dissipation is; the ambient rating, not theta-JA, is the binding constraint in most designs.
  - If the part must run near its rating, add a ground pour under/around the package, use a through-hole socket only if necessary (sockets add roughly 5 to 15 degC/W), and keep the two VCC/GND pin pairs (pins 7/8 and 20/21) tied to the plane with short, wide traces.
  - theta-JA is not a die-attach or airflow-independent constant: forced air of 1 m/s to 2 m/s typically cuts it 20 to 30 percent; an enclosure with no venting can double it.
